claims.text: High configurational entropy intrinsically produces sluggish diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Strong inter-element bonding contributes to sluggish diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sluggish diffusion governs both structural and chemical stability at high temperatures by retarding atomic mobility.
Retarded atomic mobility impedes phase separation and chemical segregation.
Inert gas condensation or rapid solidification can produce a single-phase, atomically mixed high-entropy nanoalloy.
An inert or reducing atmosphere minimizes oxidation during high-temperature exposure.
High mixing entropy suppresses grain growth and phase separation by reducing diffusivity.
The presence of many different atomic species in the lattice means that no single element dominates.
The presence of many different atomic species slows overall diffusion kinetics.
Strong inter-element bonding increases the effective mixing-enthalpy barrier for atomic rearrangement.
Sluggish diffusion combined with strong inter-element bonding stabilizes the structure and minimizes chemical segregation at high temperatures.
After equivalent high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will show less grain coarsening than a lower-entropy nanoalloy.
After equivalent high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will show slower phase separation than a lower-entropy nanoalloy.
After equivalent high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a more uniform chemical composition than a lower-entropy nanoalloy.
The prediction is expected to apply at 800–1000 °C when nanoscale feature sizes make diffusion effects measurable.
At sufficiently high temperatures, alternative diffusion or segregation mechanisms may invalidate the prediction.
Oxidation-dominated behavior may invalidate the prediction.
The magnitude of diffusion retardation and stability may depend on surface effects, elemental makeup, and processing route.
